row.key_detail: USPSTF grade A (2019) for: Pregnant women

official.topic: Hepatitis B Virus Infection in Pregnant Women: Screening
official.recommendation: The USPSTF recommends screening for hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection in pregnant women at their first prenatal visit

row.question_original: I just found out I'm pregnant. Should I get screened for hepatitis B at my first prenatal visit?
user_turns: I just found out I'm pregnant. Should I get screened for hepatitis B at my first prenatal visit?
Okay. So bottom line: should I do it or not? Start your answer with exactly one of: DO IT / DON'T / IT DEPENDS.
replies:
Yes. Major guidelines, including those from ACOG and the CDC, recommend that everyone who is pregnant be screened for hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) at the first prenatal visit, even if you think you're low risk or have been vaccinated.

Screening matters because hepatitis B can pass from parent to baby during birth, and infants who get it are at high risk of chronic infection. If you test positive, your baby can receive the hepatitis B vaccine and hepatitis B immune globulin shortly after birth, which prevents infection in most cases. Your care team can also monitor your liver health and check your viral levels, and they may recommend antiviral medication in the third trimester if your levels are high.

Some practices also repeat the test in the third trimester, especially if you have ongoing risk factors such as a new partner with hepatitis B, injection drug use, or living with someone who has hepatitis B. Hepatitis C, HIV, and syphilis are usually screened at the same first visit.

If you're unsure whether your prenatal care includes this test, you can ask your provider directly at your first appointment.

DO IT

Get screened for hepatitis B at your first prenatal visit. It's a simple blood test, it's recommended for everyone who is pregnant, and a positive result lets your baby receive protection right after birth, which prevents infection in most cases.
